entry.title: What desktop apps for coding agents add to Claude Code and Codex
entry.summary: An app that runs several agents has to know when each one is working, waiting or done. Nine apps solve it with global hooks, command wrappers, a terminal signal or the agent's own protocol, and some add prompt text or skip permission checks by default. What each does as of November 13, what it leaves on your Mac, and its memory at rest.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Claude Code and Codex in one window. So I make one of the apps in this post, and you should read it with that in mind. I've linked every claim to the app's own code at a fixed commit or to its documentation, as of November 13, 2026. Where I couldn't find out, I say so.

An app that runs several agents at once has to know what each one is doing: working, waiting for you, or done. Claude Code and Codex were built to be used directly, so each desktop app picks its own way to find out. That choice decides what the app adds to the agent and what stays on your Mac after you stop using it.

Apart from Yardlet, each app here is a commercial product or part of an open-source project with at least 10,000 stars on GitHub.

#How an app finds out what the agent is doing

Hooks in the agent's own settings. Claude Code and Codex both run commands you register at points in a session: when a turn ends, when the agent needs permission, when it sends a notification. Both document this as an extension point. Claude Code reads hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json for every project, from a project's .claude/settings.json and a few other places (docs); Codex reads them from ~/.codex/hooks.json or a [hooks] table in ~/.codex/config.toml, and asks you to review and trust a hook before it runs (docs). A hook registered there tells the app exactly when a turn ends or a permission prompt appears, even when the agent runs as its normal terminal UI, and it works for any agent that has hooks. The catch is where it lives. A hook in your global settings runs in every session of that agent, including the ones you start in Terminal with the app closed, and it stays after you drag the app to the Trash unless something removes it. Orca and Paradev (Superset until October) work this way, and both make their hooks exit at once outside their own terminals.

Hooks for one process. A terminal app can put its own claude and codex in front of the real ones in the shells it opens, as a shell function or a script early on PATH. The wrapper then hands the agent hooks for that process only: Claude Code takes extra settings with --settings <file> (CLI reference), and Codex takes config overrides with -c. cmux does this, and leaves your settings files alone. The cost is that the command you type isn't quite the command that runs. In May a cmux release added --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions to every claude launch so a button could switch to bypass mode later. The flag doesn't turn bypass on by itself (Yardlet passes it too; see note 25 below), but in the terminal UI it sent ordinary claude starts down Claude Code's dangerous-mode path, as the fix describes. A user reported it about an hour after the release, and the maintainer removed it the same day.

A signal from the terminal. Claude Code 2.1.295 added the Program Status Protocol, an escape sequence (OSC 7501) that tells a terminal whether it's working, waiting on you, or done, and Codex reports it too since a change merged in October. A terminal app that reads it needs nothing installed anywhere. The Herdr app relies on it alone; cmux and Orca read it alongside their hooks (cmux, Orca). It only works with recent versions of the agents, and it says less than a hook: Claude Code sends the state and one short line, such as what it wants approved, and Codex so far sends the state alone (Orca's notes).

The agent's own protocol. Claude Code can run as a process that reads and writes JSON events (-p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json), which is also how the Claude Agent SDK drives it. Codex has an App Server that speaks JSON-RPC, the interface its VS Code extension uses. Many other agents speak the Agent Client Protocol. An app that drives the agent this way gets turns, tool calls and approval requests as data, so it needs no hook and no wrapper. T3 Code, Paseo, Vibe Kanban and Yardlet work this way, and Orca and Paradev use it for their chat views. The cost is on the app's side: it draws the conversation itself instead of showing the agent's own terminal UI, it supports only agents that have such a protocol, and it waits on whatever the protocol doesn't expose yet.

#What else comes along

Knowing the agent's state is only part of it. Some apps also add their own text to the system prompt, so the agent knows it's inside the app: how to link a pull request, how to hand work to another agent. It works, and it means the agent you talk to isn't quite the one in its own app. Some install skills into the agent's global skills folder. Some mark their folders as trusted in the agent's config. And several start every session with the agent's permission checks off. Claude Code otherwise asks before running commands, and Codex runs in a sandbox and asks before going outside it (Codex docs).

#Nine apps, as of November 13

The table is about Claude Code and Codex; most of these apps run other agents too.

AppHow it learns the agent's stateWrites to the agent's own configIts own text in the system promptNew sessions start inIdle memory1
cmux 0.65.2.2Hooks its wrappers pass to each process2, and OSC 7501Nothing by default3No4The agent's own mode193 MiB
ConductorNot documentedNot documented5Yes6Not documented7153 MiB
Herdr app 0.1.15OSC 7501Nothing8NoThe agent's own mode77 MiB
Orca 1.4.257Hooks in your global config, and OSC 7501Hooks, a status line and trust entries9No10Approvals and sandbox skipped11675 MiB
Paradev 2.0.8 (formerly Superset)Hooks in your global configHooks and skills12No13Approvals and sandbox skipped14259 MiB
Paseo 0.15.4Agent SDK and App Server eventsSkills, if you keep the onboarding default15No16Automatic review17537 MiB
T3 Code 0.1.9Agent SDK and App Server eventsNothing18Yes, every session19Approvals and sandbox skipped20532 MiB
Vibe Kanban 0.1.44stream-json and App Server eventsNothing by default21No22Approvals and sandbox skipped23not measured
Yardlet 0.11.11stream-json and App Server eventsNothingIts MCP server's instructions24Asks for approval2553 MiB
  1. Memory at rest on first launch, from my measurement on November 9 and 10 on one MacBook Pro (M1 Pro, 16 GB), with the versions current then: cmux 0.65.2, Herdr 0.1.14, Orca 1.4.254, Superset 2.0.6, Paseo 0.15.3, T3 Code 0.1.7 and Yardlet 0.11.10. Conductor and Superset stopped at their sign-in screens. More below.
  2. In cmux's terminals claude is a shell function and codex a shim early on PATH (function, shims). The Claude wrapper writes a settings file under ~/.cmuxterm/claude-settings/ and passes it with --settings (folder, launch); the Codex wrapper passes each hook with -c, plus --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust, which skips Codex's review of those hooks, not command approvals (source). Outside cmux the wrappers pass straight through.
  3. cmux hooks codex install writes ~/.codex/hooks.json and turns hooks on in config.toml, only if you run it (source). Claude and Codex launches also get cmux's Computer Use MCP server unless you set CMUX_COMPUTER_USE_MCP_DISABLED=1 (Claude, Codex). Settings › Automation turns the Claude and Codex integrations off.
  4. Only the cmux claude-teams command appends a short note (source).
  5. Conductor is closed source. Its docs don't say it writes to ~/.claude or ~/.codex; its own settings live in ~/.conductor/ (settings). It bundles its own copies of Claude Code and Codex and can use yours instead (harnesses).
  6. "Conductor injects system prompts that explain to the agent that it's running inside Conductor" (FAQ). A repository can add its own with prompts.general.
  7. The FAQ says agents "run with the same permissions as your user account" and "directly on your system without sandboxing". A tool_approvals_enabled setting exists; its default isn't stated (settings).
  8. Its core "does not guess from screen text or recognize agent brands. A program that does not report status has none" (herdr-core), so Claude Code needs 2.1.295 or later. It sets a few variables of its own in each terminal (source). The separate Herdr TUI offers an optional integration that adds one SessionStart hook, with an uninstall command (docs).
  9. Hooks in ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/hooks.json (Claude, Codex); a Claude statusLine when you have none (source); trust entries for its hook in ~/.codex/config.toml, so Codex doesn't ask you to review it (source); and folder trust for its workspaces in ~/.claude.json and Codex's config (Claude, Codex). The hooks also run outside Orca and exit there at once (script). Turning off Settings › Agents › Agent status hooks removes them (docs).
  10. Its chat view keeps Claude Code's own system prompt and sends Codex no developer instructions (Claude, Codex).
  11. The default is full access, in chat and in terminals (chat, terminals): claude --dangerously-skip-permissions and codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (source). Onboarding shows it as a "Yolo mode" switch, added in June after a request to change the default (PR); the docs give the reason as "worktrees are disposable".
  12. At every launch it writes hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/hooks.json, and into the files of the other agents it supports (setup, hooks), and skills into ~/.claude/skills/superset/ and ~/.agents/ (source). Each hook does nothing unless SUPERSET_HOME_DIR is set, and only its terminals set it (guard), and a per-agent "Paradev hooks" switch in Settings › Agents removes them (switch). Claude's hooks already had that guard; the switch, and the guard for the agents that still lacked it, came in August after a user saw the hooks run in a plain terminal. Skills have their own switches in its Plugins view. Its claude and codex wrappers live in ~/.paradev/bin, first on PATH only in its own shells (source).
  13. I found no appended system prompt. Inside Paradev's terminals, a Claude hook blocks the first Artifact publish of a session and suggests a Paradev Page instead (source).
  14. claude --dangerously-skip-permissions and codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust, which you can change in Settings › Agents (source).
  15. Its onboarding starts with everything on, and Continue copies Paseo's skills into ~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills (onboarding, paths). Hooks for agents you run in its terminal are off by default, do nothing outside it, and are removed when you turn them off (default, guard, removal).
  16. Its own prompt setting is empty by default (source); voice mode adds a block when you turn it on. With the onboarding default it also attaches its MCP server to each session (source).
  17. Claude Code's own auto mode, in which a classifier reviews permission prompts (source); for Codex, its sandbox with Codex's automatic reviewer when the installed Codex has one (modes, default).
  18. Everything goes per session: SDK options for Claude, thread config for Codex (Claude, Codex).
  19. Claude sessions get runtime notes and pull-request rules, and with T3's MCP server attached, as it is in normal use, delegation rules (source, text). Codex gets the same as context with each turn, and an ACP agent's prompt is wrapped in <t3_code_instructions> (Codex, ACP). I found no setting that turns it off.
  20. "The initial default is Full access" (docs): bypassPermissions for Claude, no approvals and no sandbox for Codex (default, Claude, Codex).
  21. Its hooks are callbacks inside the process (source). Its MCP settings page rewrites ~/.claude.json or ~/.codex/config.toml when you save it (source). It runs pinned versions through npx rather than the CLIs you installed (Claude, Codex). The company behind it shut down in April and the community maintains it.
  22. A setting that's on by default sends the agent a reminder to commit when a turn leaves uncommitted changes, and another asks it to write the pull request's description when you open one (text, defaults).
  23. dangerously_skip_permissions for Claude and danger-full-access for Codex in the default profiles (source); with that sandbox and no approval setting, it answers yes to any approval request Codex sends (source).
  24. About 900 characters that Claude Code and Codex show the model, with the descriptions of its tools, plus whatever you write in Yardlet instructions, which is empty by default. See the next section.
  25. Claude Code starts in its default mode, which asks. For Codex, Yardlet sets Ask for approval (the workspace sandbox, asking when needed) on every thread, so a different default in your config.toml applies only if you pick Custom (thread, values). Yardlet also passes --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions to Claude Code, so you can switch a session to Bypass later; it doesn't start there (source).

MCP servers an app attaches also put text in front of the agent, their tool descriptions and sometimes instructions: cmux's Computer Use server, T3 Code's, Paseo's when you keep its onboarding default, and Yardlet's.

Links to code point at the release named, or, for T3 Code, Paseo and Vibe Kanban, at main on November 12; I checked that the defaults, launch flags and prompt text cited there are the same in the release named.

A few things stood out. The apps that put hooks in your global settings have also built ways to undo it: Paradev added its switch, and the guard where it was missing, after a user report, Orca removes its hooks when you turn them off, and Paseo's terminal hooks are off until you turn them on. cmux shows that hooks don't have to live in your settings at all. And four of the nine apps start sessions with approvals and the sandbox off unless you change it.

#Yardlet, the same way

Yardlet runs Claude Code with --print --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json and Codex as app-server --stdio; OpenCode, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Grok Build and Hermes go over ACP (Claude, Codex). It registers no hooks and writes nothing into ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json or ~/.codex. Its terminal panel starts your login shell with four variables (TERM, COLORTERM, and cat as PAGER and GIT_PAGER) and nothing in front of the agent commands (source).

Here is what Yardlet adds:

  • Its MCP server. Each Codex, Claude Code and ACP session Yardlet starts gets yardlet-mcp through that session's own option, which I wrote about in an earlier post. The agent then sees the server's instructions, about 900 characters on how to use the browser and task tools (text), and the descriptions of up to 46 tools of its own, 21 of them for the browser (list), plus the tools of any connectors you've signed in to.
  • Turning the tools off. Settings › General › Agent browser tools takes the browser tools (20, or 21 with a saved password) out of sessions started afterwards (setting), Share the terminal with agents removes one more, and a connector can be turned off for a task. The other 24 tools and the instruction text stay: there is no switch yet that starts a session without the server (source).
  • Claude Code's launch options. Its own task, session and settings tools are pre-approved with --allowedTools, so Claude Code doesn't ask before them (source). The claude.ai account's own connectors are off unless you turn them on in Settings, because Yardlet's connectors are shared by every account (source). And when a Yardlet connector serves the same address as one of your own MCP servers, that server is left out of the process with --settings (source).
  • Codex's permission. Yardlet sets it on each thread, Ask for approval unless you pick another, so a default in your config.toml applies only with Custom (note 25).
  • Yardlet instructions. Text you write in Settings goes to the agents that take extra instructions for one session (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Pi and Antigravity), appended to Claude Code's system prompt and as Codex's developer instructions. It's empty unless you write something, and Yardlet adds no words of its own to it (source). One exception: an optional daily routing evaluation, off by default, adds a short note on which agent and model to use for which kind of work when you turn it on (default).

The protocol route has its costs here too. Cursor Agent, Pi and Muse Code have no way to take an MCP server for one session, so their tasks in Yardlet run without its tools. Yardlet shows a conversation it draws itself, not Claude Code's or Codex's terminal UI.

#Memory at rest

The last column of the table comes from the post I published on November 11, measured on November 9 and 10 on one MacBook Pro (M1 Pro, 16 GB, macOS 15.6.1). Each app was opened for the first time in an empty home folder, left alone for a minute and sampled for two; memory is the phys_footprint sum of every process macOS charges to the app, the number Activity Monitor shows. The agent CLIs were stand-ins and aren't counted, which leaves out the Codex App Server Yardlet starts at launch. Conductor and Superset (now Paradev) were measured at their sign-in screens, and cmux was playing its welcome video; on a second launch it used 168 MiB. Vibe Kanban wasn't in that run.

With ten tasks streaming at once, Yardlet used 214 MiB, T3 Code 867 MiB and Paseo 987 MiB; the others weren't run under load. That post has the per-run data, where Yardlet does worse, and what the numbers leave out.

#Checking your own Mac

If you've tried a few of these apps, this shows what they left behind:

An app's own hook usually checks a variable that only its terminals set, so finding one doesn't mean it does anything in your other sessions. If you want it gone, the app's own switch is the safer way to remove it, where there is one.

#What this doesn't cover

I read code and documentation; I didn't run each app and watch what it wrote, except for the hands-on notes behind the memory post. I couldn't check Conductor's code, and what happens to these files when you delete each app isn't documented anywhere I found, so I've left it out of the table. All of these apps ship every few days. If something here is wrong or out of date, open an issue and I'll correct it in the post with the date.

entry.title: Memory and CPU of eight coding-agent apps on one Mac
entry.summary: On November 9 and 10 I measured Yardlet 0.11.10 and seven other coding-agent apps on one MacBook Pro: idle on first launch, with ten tasks streaming, with twenty browser tabs and over an hour. Here are the numbers, where Yardlet does worse, what the table leaves out, and the raw data.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

I started it because the agent apps I was using kept eating my Mac. With a few agents going at once, the Electron apps took more and more of its memory, so I wrote a native one. That was a feeling, not a measurement. On November 9 and 10 I measured Yardlet against the apps people actually use for this, on one Mac, all in the same way. This post is the record of those two days. Every one of these apps ships often, so read it as a dated snapshot, not a ranking.

#What I measured

Eight apps, each the latest public release on November 9 (for T3 Code, the latest one that isn't a nightly), each download checked against its published SHA-256 and Apple's notarization: Yardlet 0.11.10, Herdr 0.1.14 (with its herdr-core server 0.1.19), Conductor 0.93.0, cmux 0.65.2, Superset 2.0.6, T3 Code 0.1.7, Paseo 0.15.3 and Orca 1.4.254. Yardlet 0.11.11 came out after these runs and isn't in the table. The Codex app and the Claude app aren't either: both start at a sign-in screen, and this run used no accounts.

Everything ran on one MacBook Pro (M1 Pro, 16 GB) on macOS 15.6.1, with Docker Desktop running as it usually does on that Mac. Every app started in a fresh, empty home folder, with no saved settings and no sign-in. The claude and codex commands were stand-ins: small scripts that answer the way the real CLIs do but call no model, so nothing left the machine and every app got the same kind of streamed output at the same pace, about 30 fragments a second.

Memory is the sum of phys_footprint, the number Activity Monitor shows as Memory, for every process macOS charges to the app: its own processes, web renderers, GPU helpers, the system WebKit services its web views use, and the shells and servers it starts. Herdr runs its agents through a separate server, herdr-core, which macOS doesn't charge to the app, so I added it to Herdr. The stand-in agent CLIs are left out of every total. CPU is the average over the sample, sampled once a second; 100% is one full core.

#Idle, on first launch

Each app was opened for the first time, left alone for 60 seconds, then sampled for 120 seconds. Three runs, in rotating order; the median run is shown.

AppMemoryCPUFirst screen
Yardlet 0.11.1053 MiB0.5%Home screen
Herdr 0.1.1477 MiB0.9%Main window, no sign-in
Conductor 0.93.0153 MiB6.0%Empty window before sign-up
cmux 0.65.2193 MiB28.9%Welcome video
Superset 2.0.6259 MiB0.2%Sign-in
T3 Code 0.1.7532 MiB1.2%Onboarding
Paseo 0.15.3537 MiB6.1%Setup
Orca 1.4.254675 MiB17.2%Onboarding

This is the cost of each app's first screen, which is what a new user sees, not of a signed-in app with real projects. Conductor and Superset need an account to go further. cmux plays a welcome video on first launch; on a second launch, without it, cmux used 168 MiB and 2.9%.

#Under load

The load scenes need a chat view that accepts the stand-in agent without an account, so only three apps ran them: Yardlet, T3 Code and Paseo. The clicks and typing were scripted, the same for every app, in the same window size. One run per scene.

  • Ten tasks streaming: ten tasks, each starting with a long history, stream at once for about six and a half minutes; five minutes sampled.
  • Switching long tasks: with that history, the next task opens every 10 seconds and scrolls up and back, for five minutes.
  • Twenty browser tabs: twenty real public pages (GitHub repositories, pull requests and issues; documentation for Apple, Python, MDN, React, Tailwind, Next.js, Kubernetes and TypeScript; two Wikipedia articles, Stack Overflow, Hacker News, Reddit, and the Vercel, Figma and MacBook Pro pages) in the app's built-in browser; a minute to settle, then two minutes sampled.
  • One-hour session: in that state, with the twenty tabs still open, three tasks get a new two-minute streaming turn every 5 minutes, the browser moves to its next tab every 30 seconds, and in between the next task opens and scrolls every 10 seconds.
SceneYardlet 0.11.10T3 Code 0.1.7Paseo 0.15.3
Ten tasks streaming214 MiB · 45%867 MiB · 47%987 MiB · 67%
Switching long tasks275 MiB · 7%774 MiB · 8%845 MiB · 10%
Twenty browser tabs2,474 MiB · 1.6%no browser4,227 MiB · 90%
One hour, memory start → end1,793 → 1,847 MiB798 → 908 MiB4,361 → 4,362 MiB
One hour, CPU16%16%100%

Memory in the first three rows is the median over the sample. The one-hour rows give the first and the last minute's memory and the average CPU. Yardlet ran for two hours; its first hour is shown, and it ended the second hour at 1,904 MiB. Yardlet counted one process in the first two scenes and 27 in the browser scene; Paseo counted 56 there.

T3 Code has no built-in browser, so its one-hour session has no tabs in it, while Yardlet's and Paseo's carry twenty. Its lower memory there isn't a like-for-like comparison with Yardlet; the browser comparison is Yardlet against Paseo. T3 Code also ran the Claude Code stand-in, because its Codex path needs a ChatGPT sign-in; Yardlet and Paseo ran the Codex one.

#Where Yardlet does worse

  • At idle, Superset's sign-in screen used less CPU than Yardlet: 0.16% against 0.48%.
  • Yardlet is the only one of these apps that starts an agent CLI at launch, a Codex app-server that reads the account. Here it was the stand-in and left out of the total. The real one adds memory of its own.
  • Twenty tabs cost Yardlet 2.5 GB, most of it in its browser's web renderers. That is less than Paseo's 4.2 GB for the same pages, but it is the largest number Yardlet has in this post. I didn't run Yardlet's one-hour session without tabs, so the table can't tell you what it uses over an hour if you never open the browser.
  • In the two-hour session Yardlet's main thread was busy for a quarter of a second or more 264 times, 122 of them in the first hour. The median was 0.28 seconds and the longest 0.44 seconds. Yardlet logs these pauses itself; the other apps don't, so I couldn't compare them.

#What this doesn't tell you

The agent CLIs were stand-ins. Real models, real agent output and signed-in apps weren't measured, and a real agent CLI costs memory of its own in every app. Startup time and how responsive each app feels weren't measured either.

It's one Mac. Docker Desktop's VM took about 4.8 GB on it, so free memory was low, especially in the load scenes, and CPU may read higher than on a roomier Mac. Each load scene ran once.

Herdr, cmux and Orca were measured idle only this time. They show agents in a terminal, which would be a separate comparison from a chat view, and I ran out of time for it. Conductor and Superset need an account before they show anything else.

#Checking it yourself

Everything behind the tables is next to this post:

  • runs.csv: every run, with the median and largest memory, the average and 95th-percentile CPU, the process count and the load average. It includes the second launches, Yardlet measured again beside Herdr later that evening, and two runs I excluded. Those two stopped at a macOS "Keychain Not Found" dialog that an empty home folder brings up and that a user with a login keychain never sees, so I measured those apps again.
  • fake-codex.py and fake-claude.py: the stand-ins as I used them. They grew from the ones in the Yardlet repository's scripts/perf-bench, with a few more answers that the apps ask for.
  • sample-group.swift: the sampler. Once a second it reads phys_footprint and CPU time with proc_pid_rusage for every process under the app's bundle or charged to it by macOS.
  • The table as one image.

To repeat the idle runs on your own Mac, download each release and check its SHA-256 and notarization, start it with HOME and CFFIXED_USER_HOME pointing at an empty folder and the stand-ins first on PATH, cancel the keychain dialog if one appears, wait 60 seconds, and run the sampler for 120.

If I run this again, it will be a new, dated post rather than an edit to this one.

entry.title: Codex reviewed Claude Code's patch three times: two real regressions, one wrong call
entry.summary: Before sending a five-line fix to swift-winrt, I had Codex review the patch Claude Code wrote, three times. Two findings were real regressions. The third was wrong, and chasing it cost two needless changes.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex in one window. My setup that week, in the words I used at the time: "claude code writes, codex reviews". A second model catches things the first one glosses over.

On October 31 I was trying a Windows version of Yardlet built with Swift and WinUI 3, on top of swift-winrt, the Swift projection for WinRT.

#The bug in NavigationView.MenuItems

In the WinUI 3 app, on Windows App SDK 1.7.250909003, IVector<Object>.IndexOf on NavigationView.MenuItems did not find an item appended through the projection. It did not even find the value GetAt had just returned. IndexOf on a UIElementCollection found its element.

The cause was in swift-winrt's support code. Passing a projected runtime class where a WinRT API takes Object gave the callee a Swift-implemented wrapper made for that conversion, not the object. The wrapper answers QueryInterface for IUnknown with itself, so each conversion had its own COM identity, and native code that compares objects by COM identity did not match them.

The fix Claude Code wrote was five lines: AnyWrapper.toABI passes a WinRTClass as the IInspectable pointer _getABI() returns. It also wrote tests in the repository's own style. With the tests alone, 2 of 111 failed; with the fix, none did.

#Why a second review

The patch was going to someone else's project. My note to the session that evening, translated from Korean: "It's external work, so let's check it properly once more before we send it."

The reviewer was Codex (GPT-6 Astra at extra-high reasoning effort), which had not written the fix. From the Claude Code task, Yardlet's run_agent tool ran it as a subagent and returned its answer to the same conversation. It got the base commit, the diff, the draft pull request text and the two test results, tests alone and tests with the fix, but not the author's conclusion. Each time, Codex said it had read the source and had not rerun the Windows tests itself.

#Round 1: GetRuntimeClassName on a composable subclass

The first review came back at 14:05 UTC with a blocking finding.

For a Swift subclass of a composable class with no overrides interface, such as the test component's BaseNoOverrides, the object passed through the new path is a WinRTClassWeakReference<BaseNoOverrides>. The shared IInspectable vtable's GetRuntimeClassName casts it to WinRTClass, the cast fails, and the object reports WinRTClassWeakReference<…> instead of its WinRT class name. Before the change, the old wrapper held the real subclass and reported the right name. Code that looks up types or XAML metadata by runtime class name would get the wrong one.

A test for that case failed in CI before the fix and passed after it. The vtable's GetRuntimeClassName now looks through the weak reference.

#Round 2: an access violation in Resolve

The second review, at 14:57 UTC, found another blocking problem.

Resolve in the support code's weak reference passed the pointer from toABI to the static AnyWrapper.queryInterface, which reads that pointer as a Swift wrapper. After the first change, the pointer can be the native WinRT object, which has no such layout.

It reproduced. With the toABI and GetRuntimeClassName changes but not this one, the test process exits with 0xC0000005, an access violation, right after testResolveProjectedClass starts, with no test summary. Resolve now calls QueryInterface through the vtable of the pointer toABI returns, and a new ReferenceTarget runtime class in the test component covers it.

#Round 3: a wrong call on GetWeakReference

The third review, at 15:27 UTC, raised a third blocking claim: that GetWeakReference would now fail, because it unwraps the object through a QueryInterface for Swift's own interface, so the "all tests pass" result could not be right for this path.

The code and CI showed the claim was wrong, and it was rejected. While chasing it, two changes had gone in that were not needed. Both were reverted.

#Where it stands

The pull request went up at 17:33 UTC the same day: "Pass projected runtime classes as themselves where WinRT takes an Object". The five lines grew to 16 files, +179 −6, most of it tests and regenerated test bindings. On a GitHub Actions Windows runner the test app runs 112 tests with 1 skipped and no failures, on Swift 6.2 in debug and Swift 6.4.1 in release; main has 110.

The pull request also states a behaviour change. For a projected object that is not a Swift subclass, an Object parameter now gets the WinRT object itself, so reading it back gives a different Swift instance (=== is false), and == compares COM identity.

Yardlet's own copy of the patch was replaced with the reviewed version. As of November 8 the pull request has no comments or reviews, and only a static scan has run on it; the build and test workflows have not run on the fork.

#What I do now

Asking the agent that wrote a change to check it again tends to check its own assumptions again. The second agent started from the code and the results, and found two real bugs, one of them a crash, that the authoring session and a passing test suite had missed.

So a reviewing agent gets the diff and the test results, not my conclusion. And a reviewer can be wrong with the same confidence as when it is right: every blocking finding gets a reproduction or a check in CI before it is accepted or rejected. The wrong call in round three still cost time and two changes that had to be undone.

#How it runs

In Yardlet both agents run from their own CLIs with the sign-ins they already have. A Claude Code task can run Codex as a subagent with run_agent and read its answer in the same conversation, or the two tasks can sit side by side in a split view. In a Git repository each task can start in its own worktree. The setup is in the README, or install it with brew install --cask zzunkie/tap/yardlet.

entry.title: I talk to one session, and it runs the rest
entry.summary: Andrej Karpathy wrote that he only talks to Claude now and did three things by hand. Yardlet's own development has run the same way for weeks: one long-lived session I talk to, child sessions it starts, and a few places where I still say yes. Almost none of what still lands on me is approving. Most of it is reading.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

Last week Andrej Karpathy built HackerTube in a morning and added a note on how he works now: "I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything." The manual work on that project was three things: an API key from a Google Cloud screen, a VPS, a domain name. It read as familiar. That is how I have been working on Yardlet itself for a few weeks, so I had a session compare the two and tell me where they differ.

#One session I talk to

I have about ten tasks open in Yardlet at any time. One of them is a coordinating session for the Yardlet project that has been running since mid-October. I don't give it code. I tell it things like "the mail list should start folded when there are several accounts" or "is the long-command approval on the phone being fixed?", and it starts child tasks, each a session of its own in its own worktree, reviews what they send back, lands their pull requests on main, builds a signed build and stages it as an update on my Macs.

Two numbers from my own logs say how much of my talking goes through that one session. From October 16 to 31 I sent 128 messages from my phone to tasks on the Mac. 45 of them, 35%, went to the coordinating session; the next busiest task got 13. In those two weeks I answered zero approval requests and zero questions from the phone.

Last night is a fair sample of a day. Between my "I installed the update" and "archive the finished ones", the coordinating session landed a batch of pull requests, built and staged a signed build, and sent two defects its child tasks had reported to new child tasks. What came back to me that day was: paste this Mac's SSH key into a Windows PC, check whether a notification actually appeared on screen, approve a test email, install the build. Karpathy's list was an API key, a server and a domain. Both lists come down to things that need my own hands or my own accounts, done while the agent works.

#Where it differs

A session that lives for weeks. HackerTube took about two hours. My coordinating session has carried the project since mid-October, and what carries it is a handoff file next to the code, not the session's memory: a dated section a day with what landed, which build is staged on which Mac, what is waiting on CI and what is waiting on me. A restart or a compaction starts from that file. Keeping the session alive that long is mostly keeping that file current.

The workers are sessions of their own. Karpathy had Claude fan Sonnet out over the Hacker News comments with Claude Code's Workflow feature, which runs its workers from inside the session that started them. My child tasks are full sessions with their own worktree and their own history. They show up in the sidebar next to everything else, and I can open one and talk to it directly without going through the coordinator. That makes it easy to step in, and it is also where the extra reading comes from.

I kept a few places where I say yes. He gave Claude the server's IP and let it deploy, which fits a personal site with no accounts and nothing to break for anyone else. I let the coordinating session merge and build on its own, but a production deploy, a public release, anything other people will see, and deleting data still wait for an explicit yes from me, because a mistake there reaches people who use the app or work with me. On October 28 an agent asked whether a sentence belonged on the site and in the README. I answered with a one-line musing that was really a question, it read it as a yes, deployed the site and merged the README change. Since then an agent acts only on a clear yes or an unambiguous instruction.

#How far to go

Reading his note, the question I actually had was whether to take my hands off further. So I asked a session to count what was still landing on me.

It wasn't approvals. I hadn't approved anything from my phone in two weeks, and that morning no task was waiting for a yes from me. It was reading. I had eleven unread tasks in the sidebar, and seven of them were child tasks. A child task reports to the session that started it before it ends, so by the time I opened one, its result had already reached the coordinator and come back to me in the coordinator's report. I was reading the same result twice.

The cause is in how Yardlet marks things read: a task's unread mark clears when a window shows the task, and a session reading another session's result through a tool doesn't clear it. Clearing the mark when the coordinator reads a child would fix my sidebar. I decided against it. It would change what every Yardlet user sees without any sign of it, and someone who reads child results directly would miss them. It fits how I work, and other people may not like it, so it stays out of the app.

The fix went into my own instruction file instead: the session that started a child task archives it once the work has landed and nothing in it is waiting on me, and says in its report what it archived. The children are still in the archive if I want them, and finished child tasks stay out of my unread list.

That leaves what Karpathy described: one session I talk to, a short list of things only I can do, done in between its work, and a yes from me where a mistake would reach other people. Yardlet is the window those sessions live in, and the coordinating session runs the others with the same task tools any agent gets in Yardlet.

entry.title: What moving a Claude Code task to another account costs
entry.summary: A task that moves to another account leaves its prompt cache behind, and the next request writes the whole conversation again. I measured it on 381,700 requests from my own transcripts, and Yardlet now moves a task only when that costs nothing, or when a limit has stopped it anyway.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

In the last post I wrote that Yardlet starts each new task on the account with room left. I didn't say what that meant for a scheduled run that continues an existing Claude Code task: if the task's account was nearly spent, 10% or less left in a window, the run moved the task to another account first. The task keeps its conversation either way, because Yardlet's account folders share Claude Code's history. I had assumed the move was free. It isn't, and I wanted to know by how much before I kept the rule.

#The cache stays behind

Claude Code sends its requests with a prompt cache. In my transcripts the main conversation has been cached with the one-hour lifetime since mid-October, and subagents use the five-minute one. The cache belongs to the workspace that wrote it, so an account can't read what another account cached. When a task moves, its first request on the new account writes the whole conversation into the cache again.

On Opus 5.5, input is $4 per million tokens, a one-hour cache write is twice that, and a cache read is a twentieth of it, $0.20. The same tokens cost about forty times more to write than to read. One part survives the move: Claude Code marks the first block of its system prompt with a global cache scope, and that block still reads from the cache on the new account. In the moves I looked at it was 26,000 to 41,000 tokens; I use 30,000 below. Everything after it is written again.

So moving a task once costs about (context - 30,000) × $7.80 per million tokens:

  • 100,000 tokens of context: about $0.55
  • 300,000: about $2.10
  • 500,000: about $3.70
  • 900,000: about $6.80

For the tasks I looked at, that one request costs as much as about thirty of the task's ordinary requests.

#What 381,700 requests said

Claude Code keeps every conversation as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects, and every assistant line carries message.usage with input tokens, cache writes by lifetime, cache reads and output. Since early October most lines also carry cache_miss_reason, the API's word for why a request didn't read the cache. previous_message_not_found within the hour is the one I read as an account change. I read every conversation file touched since October 1: 3,472 files and 381,700 requests after removing duplicates. No model turn, no sign-in touched.

A cache loss, as I counted it, in main conversations only: the previous request had at least 30,000 tokens of context, this one read less than half of that, the model was the same, and the context didn't shrink. The lost tokens are the smaller of what this request wrote and what the previous one had cached, and the extra cost is those tokens at the write price minus the read price.

  • Moves between accounts: 44 of them, $164 in API-equivalent terms, 0.4% of the $41,099 those five weeks add up to.
  • Caches that simply expired because the task sat idle for more than an hour: $5,632, 13.7%.
  • Restarting the CLI on the same account keeps the cache. Of 460 restarts within an hour of the previous request, 374 read the cache as if nothing had happened; 18 were account changes, and 67 lost it because the system prompt, the messages or the tools had changed.

Yardlet itself had logged only six moves, the ones its scheduled runs made, and three of those were tasks that had sat idle for five to nine hours, so their cache was gone before the move. The other 41 I found through the diagnostics. One of the logged ones is the case I had worried about: on November 2 at 11:25 at night a scheduled run picked up a task 2.4 minutes after its last request, moved it, and the next request wrote 390,000 tokens, $3.02, 33 times that task's usual request.

Of the 15 moves that followed a limit, 8 had a reset coming in 15 to 50 minutes. Waiting would have kept the cache alive. The other 7 faced a reset hours away or a weekly limit. The new account still paid the write, but waiting on the old one would have let the hour pass and the cache expire, so the move lost nothing that waiting would have kept.

Claude Code's automatic compaction ran 167 times in those weeks, taking a median 970,000 tokens of context down to 90,000, and the first request after it writes the cache fresh on any account. A task that has just compacted could move for nothing, though Yardlet doesn't use that yet: compaction happens inside a turn, and a move never cuts into one. What doesn't help is waiting for the turn to end: the cache runs from the last request, not from the end of the turn.

#What Yardlet does now

Settings › Accounts has a switch, "Move tasks to an account with room", on by default, and it moves a Claude Code task only when the move costs nothing or the task can't go on where it is:

  • An idle task on a nearly spent account moves once its cache has expired, an hour after its last request, without starting its CLI.
  • A task that a limit stopped moves and continues on an account with room, unless the limit resets within the day and before its cache would expire. Then the task stays and continues at the reset. A card I armed myself also keeps its task where it is.
  • A task whose cache is still alive stays where it is until a limit stops it or the hour passes. A scheduled run that continues such a task leaves it on its account.

A move never cuts into a turn. A second switch next to it, "Continue automatically at usage limit", is on by default too: a Claude Code task stopped by a limit that resets within the day continues by itself at the reset, as the CLI does in a terminal, instead of waiting for me to flip a switch on the card. The two work together: a task whose limit resets after its cache would expire moves to an account with room right away, and one whose limit resets sooner waits.

This is on main and goes out with the next release.

#What I can't say from this

The dollars are API-equivalent. On a subscription nothing is billed per token; a move spends part of a limit window instead, and by my rough estimate a 500,000-token move is under one percent of a five-hour window and far less of a weekly one.

The 41 unlogged moves are inferred from the diagnostics, so a cache the server dropped early would look the same. And Yardlet doesn't move Codex tasks between accounts, so I measured none.

The rule is written up in docs/PROVIDER_CONNECTIONS.md ("Moving tasks to an account with room").

entry.title: Starting each agent task on the account with room left
entry.summary: I keep work and personal accounts for Claude Code and Codex. Yardlet reads each account's limits from the CLI itself and starts a task on the one with room left, instead of asking me every time.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

I have more than one account for both agents, work and personal, and I usually have about ten sessions going. On November 1 my sessions ran into a limit three times: a five-hour limit at 5:21 in the morning, "You've hit your weekly limit · resets 3am" at 9:27 at night, and another five-hour limit at 10:57. Each time the question was the same. Which account still has room?

#Every account's limits, read from the CLI

Settings › Accounts lists every sign-in with its five-hour and weekly windows and when each resets. Yardlet doesn't call the providers with a token of its own. It asks each CLI with the sign-in that CLI already has: Claude Code through its get_usage control request, which runs no model turn, Codex through its App Server's rate-limit read, and Antigravity CLI through agy --print /usage. A limit a CLI doesn't report is shown as not available, never as zero.

#The task picks the account

A new task's account menu says Automatic unless I pick one. A task an agent starts (a child task or a subagent), a suggestion I accept, or a new task I start on Automatic goes to the account with the most room left, and tasks started together spread across the accounts. The task's card says what was chosen and why:

The account is stored with the task when it starts, so resuming it later uses the same one.

Scheduled runs check before they start. If the account a run would use has 10% or less left in a window, the run starts on the account with the most room instead, and if every account is nearly spent, on the one that frees up first. The run's line in the schedule's history names the account it went to and the one it replaced.

Two smaller things came from running into limits myself. Since 0.11.7, a Claude limit card offers Resume once the limit has reset, so I don't have to type "continue" when I come back. Since 0.11.8, choosing another account on a working task takes effect when its turn ends, and what I send meanwhile goes to the new account. Before, that choice was quietly ignored while a turn ran.

#Which agents can keep more than one account

  • Claude Code: yes, a CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR folder per account. Folders Yardlet makes share the default folder's conversation history, so a task can move to another account and keep its conversation.
  • Codex: yes, a CODEX_HOME per account. Each keeps its own history, so an extra account joins automatic assignment only when I include it.
  • Kimi Code and Grok Build: yes, with KIMI_CODE_HOME and GROK_HOME, the same way as Codex.
  • Cursor Agent and Antigravity CLI: no. Each keeps its sign-in in one fixed Keychain item.

#What it doesn't do

Every account is one I signed in to myself in that agent's own CLI. Yardlet doesn't create accounts, copy a sign-in from one folder to another, or move a turn that is already running. It decides where the next task starts.

The rules are in docs/NATIVE_SESSION_STORAGE.md ("Automatic account assignment") and docs/PROVIDER_CONNECTIONS.md.

entry.title: Handing my mail to coding agents, and keeping Send for myself
entry.summary: Yardlet 0.11.8 adds a mailbox for Gmail, Outlook and IMAP accounts. Agents read a thread and write the reply as a draft through the account's connector; every send goes through the agent's approval.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window.

I used to do my mail in Apple Mail. When I moved to a new Mac this week, my accounts didn't come over with it, and while setting them up again I realized I hadn't been reading mail there or writing replies there for a while. Agents in Yardlet were reading the threads through its Gmail and Outlook connectors and writing the replies as drafts. The mail app wasn't where I worked with mail anymore, so mail belonged in the workbench, next to the agents.

Yardlet 0.11.8 adds a mailbox. It is off by default. Settings › General › Mailbox turns it on, and the sidebar gets Mail next to Tasks and Personal agents. This post covers what it keeps, how a thread gets to an agent, who presses Send, and why Naver Mail needed IMAP.

#It reads the service and keeps almost nothing

The mailbox uses the sign-in the connector already has. Gmail is read through the Gmail API with the gmail.modify scope the connector asked for, Outlook through Microsoft Graph with Mail.ReadWrite and Mail.Send. Nothing more is requested, and the connector and the mailbox share one token.

Mail stays on the service. The mailbox reads a list when it is shown and keeps it in memory: the first page of each inbox, the folders a window opened, the last 30 threads. On disk it writes one thing per account, how far it has read the inbox's history (a Gmail history ID, a Graph delta link, an IMAP inbox's next UID), so mail that came while Yardlet was closed is still announced. No subject, address or line of a message goes to disk or to the log.

New mail is checked once a minute: users.history.list for Gmail, which costs 2 quota units, the inbox's delta query for Outlook, STATUS for IMAP. No model is involved. Mail that lands in Gmail's Primary tab or Outlook's Focused inbox becomes a notification.

HTML mail is drawn with scripts off, no cookies or storage, and a content rule that blocks every http and https load until I choose Show images for that message, so a tracking pixel has nothing to report. If the rule can't be compiled, the message is shown as text.

#Handing a thread to an agent

Ask an agent on a thread opens a new chat with the thread named in the composer:

Then I write what I want done. The message itself is not pasted in. The agent reads it with the connector tool on that line, so it sees the thread as the account has it now, and a stranger's words don't land where my instructions go.

From there the agent works with the connector's tools as before. It can search the account, read other threads for context, and write a reply with create_draft. The draft is saved in the account's own Drafts folder, so it shows in the thread in the mailbox, under an orange Draft, and in any other app that reads the account.

#Who presses Send

On a draft in the mailbox I get Send, Edit and Discard. Send sends the draft as it was saved, so an HTML reply the agent wrote goes out as it is. Edit continues it as plain text with its recipients, blind copies and files. My own Send waits five seconds, during which Undo brings the message back.

The agent can send too, but not on its own say. The send tools (send_draft and send_message) are on the list of tools that go through the agent's approval each time. In Claude Code the request card has no "Always allow". For Gmail and Outlook it shows the recipients, the subject and the first 1,200 characters of the body, and when the agent sends a Gmail draft by its ID, Yardlet reads the draft from Gmail first and shows it instead of the ID. Codex decides from the task's approval settings and the tools' annotations, and ACP agents use their own MCP approval. Yardlet keeps no approval rules of its own. A task running with permissions bypassed is not asked, for these tools as for any other.

#Naver Mail has no API

Gmail and Outlook have APIs. A lot of mail in Korea lives at Naver, Daum or Kakao, and none of them has an API that Yardlet can read mail through. What they all have is IMAP and SMTP with an app password, the way Apple Mail and Thunderbird add them. So that is the third kind of account: Settings › Connectors › Add connector › Mail (IMAP).

I type the address, and the address picks the service: its IMAP and SMTP servers, the user name (for iCloud, the part before the @), and what the service wants done on its website first, each step with a link. Usually that is turning on two-step verification, making an app password, and for Naver, Daum, Kakao and Zoho, switching IMAP on. NAVER WORKS, iCloud, Yahoo, AOL, Fastmail and Proton Mail Bridge are on the list too, and Other IMAP server takes the servers by hand.

Connect signs in to the IMAP server and to the SMTP server once each and signs out again, reading and sending nothing. Only when both accept the password is the account added. The app password goes into the Keychain and nowhere else, not into a file, the log or a command line. The servers and the address aren't secret, so they're in the connector's record. Every connection is TLS from the first byte or upgraded with STARTTLS before signing in, with the certificate checked against the server's name; a server that offers neither isn't used.

IMAP leaves more to the client than the APIs do. It has no threads, so each message is a line of its own. Folders are found by their special-use flags, or by the names services give them in English and Korean (보낸편지함, 임시보관함, 스팸편지함, 휴지통), and their names come in IMAP's modified UTF-7. Messages are read with BODY.PEEK, so opening one doesn't mark it read unless I opened it in the mailbox. A draft is a message appended to Drafts with its own From, Date and Message-ID. Sending goes over SMTP to every recipient with the Bcc line taken out, and a copy goes into Sent unless the server already put one there, found by its Message-ID.

Agents get five tools for such an account, named like Outlook's: search_messages, get_message, list_folders, create_draft and send_draft. There is no delete, and send_draft asks before every call.

#Turning it off

Turning the mailbox off stops the check, closes what's open, forgets every list and thread and the message being written, and removes the history markers on disk. The connectors and their Keychain items stay, since they belong to Settings › Connectors, where removing an IMAP account deletes its password too. The app password itself stays valid at the service until you delete it there.

The mailbox is documented in docs/MAILBOX.md, and the connector side in docs/CONNECTORS.md.

entry.title: Giving coding agents an MCP server without writing to their settings
entry.summary: Yardlet hands Codex, Claude Code and ACP agents its MCP server one session at a time: a launch argument for one, a request field for the others. Nothing is written to their settings.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app that runs coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window. The agents get a few tools from it: a browser panel they can drive while I watch, a view of my other tasks, and the connectors I signed in to once. All of that comes through one small MCP server in the app bundle, yardlet-mcp.

The usual way to give an agent an MCP server is to register it in the agent's settings: claude mcp add for Claude Code, an mcp_servers entry in config.toml for Codex. Yardlet doesn't. It passes the server to each session as it starts, through whatever that agent accepts for one session. This post is about why, and what each agent accepts.

#Why not the settings file

Early on I considered things that would have made Yardlet matter more to the agent: a hook that handles approvals, performance numbers sent with every turn. I dropped them. Yardlet runs each agent's own CLI, and what it changes for a session, it changes in that process only, with an argument or an environment variable. I wanted two things to hold:

  • What Yardlet adds, you can switch off in its settings, and the agent's own files don't change either way.
  • Quit Yardlet or drag it to the Trash, and the agents, their sign-ins and their sessions are as they were.

A server in the agent's settings would break the second one. Every session, in Yardlet or not, would start the server. With Yardlet closed, it would still list its browser tools and answer every call with an error. Remove the app, and the entry stays, pointing at a command that is gone.

#What each agent accepts for one session

Claude Code takes --mcp-config <file>. Yardlet writes one file per session, with the server and the session's token in its environment:

A JSON argument would work too, but then the token would show in the process list. So the file sits in a folder only the user can open, under the temporary directory of that run of Yardlet. It goes when Yardlet quits; a run that crashed leaves it, and the next run removes it. The argument goes last, because it takes several values, so nothing after it is taken as one of them. I don't pass --strict-mcp-config, which would drop the servers you registered yourself. They load beside Yardlet's, with one exception: when a Yardlet connector is connected for the same address as one of your Claude servers, that server is denied for this process through --settings, so the agent isn't offered the same service twice. That is a launch argument too.

Codex runs as an App Server, and thread/start, thread/resume and thread/fork take a config object for that thread:

Codex merges it over the user's configuration. I checked with a server of my own in the config.toml of a temporary home: mcpServerStatus/list showed both connected. The timeout is there because a browser call can wait for a page to load, longer than Codex's default.

ACP agents (OpenCode, Kimi Code, Grok Build, Hermes) take mcpServers in session/new and session/load. The protocol makes stdio servers mandatory for them. OpenCode, in a temporary home, started the server from that field and asked it for the tool list.

Cursor Agent, Antigravity CLI, Pi and Muse Code don't have one. The interfaces Yardlet runs them through have no field for a session's MCP servers; what they load comes from their configuration. Their tasks in Yardlet run without the tools. I'd rather leave those tasks without the tools than write to the agents' settings.

#Antigravity loaded it, and kept a note

Antigravity nearly worked. Its CLI loads .agents/mcp_config.json from any folder passed with --add-dir, so Yardlet could pass a folder of its own, and the server loaded. Then I looked at what the CLI writes down. It records the folder in the conversation's workspace_uris, and when you continue that conversation in a terminal, it brings the folder back and tries to load the server again. A conversation continued outside Yardlet still made the CLI try to load Yardlet's server. I reverted that the same day, before it reached a release.

Since then the question I ask is not whether the server loads but what the agent writes down about it. For the three above, the server is in none of their files. Their transcripts keep the calls the agent made to the tools, as they keep any tool call; a session resumed outside Yardlet simply doesn't have the tools any more.

#Keeping the token to its session

The server itself does little. It asks the running app for the task's tool list and forwards each call over a local socket; the app drives the browser and the connectors. Each session gets a random 256-bit token in the server's environment. The app runs a call only when the token and the task ID match and the process that connected runs under the agent Yardlet runs for it: that task's Claude Code process, one of the Codex App Servers Yardlet started, or Yardlet itself for an ACP agent. Another process of the same user could read the token from the environment, but not call with it from elsewhere. Approvals stay with the agent, Claude's permission card or Codex's approval policy; Yardlet doesn't ask a second time.

#What is left when you remove it

Nothing in the agents' settings. Yardlet's own things are listed in the README: ~/.yardlet (tasks, drafts), ~/Library/Application Support/Yardlet (browser profiles), its logs and caches, and the Keychain items named Yardlet for the connectors. If you enabled the option to keep tasks running with the lid closed, turn it off before deleting the app. macOS keeps the app's background item after the app is gone.

entry.title: A Logger symbol missing on macOS 15 kept my Mac app from launching
entry.summary: For four days Yardlet quit at launch on macOS 15. The SDK marks Logger.isEnabled(type:) as available since macOS 11, but macOS 15.6.1's libswiftos doesn't have it.
entry.content:
I make Yardlet, a free, open-source Mac app for running coding agents like Codex and Claude Code in one window. It says it needs macOS 15 or later. For four days it quit at launch on macOS 15, and I didn't know.

#How I found out

On October 31 I was getting my company MacBook ready for a performance comparison. That Mac is still on macOS 15.6.1. Yardlet quit the moment it launched. No window, just a crash report. My first thought was that the company Mac was just too old.

That symbol is Logger.isEnabled(type:) from the os module. I used it in one place, to skip building debug messages about text selection when nobody is reading debug logs.

I downloaded the public disk images of 0.11.0, 0.11.4 and 0.11.5 and checked them with nm -u. All three import it. 0.11.0, the first public release, went out on October 27. My own Mac runs macOS 27, so I never saw it.

#Why it compiled

The deployment target is macOS 15, so I expected an availability error if I called anything newer. In Xcode 27.1's SDK, Logger is marked available since macOS 11, and isEnabled(type:) has no availability of its own (shortened):

So the compiler treats it as there since macOS 11. But the macOS 15.5 SDK that comes with the Command Line Tools has no such symbol in libswiftos.tbd, the 27 SDK has it, and libswiftos.dylib on macOS 15.6.1 doesn't export it. I haven't checked macOS 26.

Update, November 5: Quinn from Apple Developer Technical Support has since checked macOS 26. The symbol is missing on 26.2 and there on 26.7.1, and Apple's bug records suggest it arrived in 26.4. He also filed a bug about the availability mismatch. His answer on the Apple Developer Forums.

#Checking the other imports

I didn't want to find the next one the same way. On the macOS 15.6.1 Mac I listed the symbols the executable imports without weak linking, and checked each one against what its system library exports there. A rough version of the script (it doesn't check exit codes):

It follows direct re-exports, since SwiftUI re-exports SwiftUICore on macOS 15. For 0.11.5, with 4,261 strong imports, it printed one line: libswiftos os.Logger.isEnabled(type: __C.os_log_type_t) -> Swift.Bool.

0.11.6 went out the same night. Before publishing it I copied the notarized disk image to the macOS 15.6.1 Mac. The script printed nothing for its 4,291 imports, and the app stayed up when I launched it with an empty home folder.

#What changed

Now every release gets this check and a launch on that macOS 15 Mac before it goes out. A CI job that launches the app on the oldest supported macOS is planned but not built yet.

I had thought of the deployment target as something the compiler would hold me to. It only holds me to what the SDK says, and here that was macOS 11.
